text:
Programs that do many things at once need a way to keep threads from stepping on each other, and the mutex is one of the most common tools for it. A mutex guards a critical section, the part of the code that touches shared data. Only one thread can hold the lock at a time, so two threads can't modify that data at the same moment. It works a bit like a bouncer at a nightclub door: one person goes in, and everyone else waits for their turn.

Mutexes can cause problems if you use them carelessly. For example, if threads acquire locks in inconsistent orders, you can end up with a deadlock, where every thread is waiting on another and none of them can proceed.

On Linux, mutexes are built on futexes. When no other thread is contending for the lock, a futex lets the program acquire and release it without making a system call, which is expensive. As a result, locking is cheap in the common case.

Whether you're writing a game, a banking app, or a startup's backend, you'll run into mutexes again and again, so it's worth learning to use them well.
